clinicalPearls: CLN8 spans a phenotypic spectrum from the comparatively mild Finnish Northern epilepsy syndrome (progressive epilepsy with intellectual disability, EPMR) to a severe Turkish variant late-infantile NCL.

Northern epilepsy begins in the early school years with generalised tonic-clonic seizures that increase in frequency, followed by slowly progressive cognitive decline; vision is relatively preserved and survival into adulthood is usual.
The variant late-infantile CLN8 phenotype presents earlier with myoclonus, motor and cognitive regression, ataxia and visual failure, a far more aggressive course.
It is caused by biallelic variants in CLN8, encoding a transmembrane protein of the endoplasmic reticulum and ER-Golgi intermediate compartment in the TLC-domain family.
CLN8 partners with CLN6 to recruit newly synthesised lysosomal enzymes for endoplasmic-reticulum-to-Golgi transport.
Stored material shows granular, curvilinear and fingerprint inclusions and is rich in subunit c of mitochondrial ATP synthase.
Diagnosis is molecular; CLN8 is not an enzyme-deficiency subtype.
A specific founder variant underlies Northern epilepsy in the Finnish population, whereas other variants worldwide tend to cause the variant late-infantile phenotype.
reference.pathophysiology: CLN8 disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic variants in CLN8 on chromosome 8p23, encoding CLN8, a multipass transmembrane protein of the endoplasmic reticulum and the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment and a member of the TLC (TRAM-LAG1-CLN8) domain family implicated in lipid and ceramide regulation. CLN8 partners with CLN6 to recruit newly synthesised lysosomal enzymes in the endoplasmic reticulum and relay them to the Golgi, so its loss reduces delivery of multiple lysosomal hydrolases and perturbs lipid homeostasis. The result is accumulation of autofluorescent ceroid-lipofuscin rich in subunit c of mitochondrial ATP synthase, with granular, curvilinear and fingerprint inclusions, and progressive neurodegeneration. Residual protein function determines severity: a Finnish founder variant produces the comparatively protracted Northern epilepsy syndrome with intellectual disability, while other variants cause a severe variant late-infantile NCL with retinal involvement.
additionalDifferentials: CLN5, CLN6 and CLN7 (MFSD8) variant late-infantile NCLs
Other genetic epilepsies with intellectual disability (for the Northern epilepsy phenotype)
Progressive myoclonic epilepsies (Unverricht-Lundborg disease, Lafora disease)
Other causes of childhood epileptic encephalopathy with regression
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic testing (CLN8 sequencing, NCL gene panel or exome sequencing)
Brain MRI for cerebellar atrophy, which may be subtle in Northern epilepsy
Electroretinography and ophthalmology (retinal involvement in the variant late-infantile form; relatively spared in Northern epilepsy)
Electron microscopy of skin or conjunctival biopsy for granular and curvilinear inclusions
redFlags: Increasingly frequent tonic-clonic seizures with insidious cognitive decline in a school-age child
Developmental regression with visual loss in the variant late-infantile form
reference.prognosis: Northern epilepsy is comparatively protracted, with seizures often lessening after puberty but persistent cognitive impairment and survival into adulthood; the variant late-infantile CLN8 phenotype is severe and shortens life to childhood or adolescence. Care is supportive.
pitfalls: Not recognising Northern epilepsy as an NCL because vision and lifespan are relatively preserved.
Assuming uniform severity across CLN8; the phenotype varies widely by variant.
Relying on enzyme assays, which are normal.
Missing the diagnosis where the founder-population context is absent.
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists, so management is supportive across the spectrum from Northern epilepsy to the variant late-infantile phenotype
Control seizures with antiepileptic drugs, noting that in Northern epilepsy seizure frequency often lessens after puberty
Manage myoclonus, ataxia and spasticity in the variant late-infantile form with appropriate antiepileptic and antispasticity agents, avoiding drugs that worsen myoclonus
Provide physiotherapy, occupational therapy and neuropsychological support for progressive cognitive impairment
Arrange ophthalmology and low-vision support in the variant late-infantile form, where vision is relatively preserved in Northern epilepsy
Support nutrition and swallowing with gastrostomy feeding as bulbar function declines in the severe phenotype
Coordinate multidisciplinary neurology, rehabilitation and palliative care
Offer genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
